clinicalPearls: The most common and most significant carpal instability pattern, resulting from disruption of the scapholunate interosseous ligament, particularly its stronger dorsal component.
The Watson scaphoid shift test reproduces dorsal pain and a clunk as the scaphoid subluxates over the dorsal rim of the radius on radial deviation.
Classic static radiographic signs are a widened scapholunate gap (Terry Thomas sign) on the PA view and a cortical ring sign from the abnormally flexed scaphoid seen end-on.
A clenched-fist PA view stresses the interval and may unmask dynamic instability not evident on standard films.
On the lateral radiograph an increased scapholunate angle indicates a dorsal intercalated segment instability (DISI) posture, with the lunate extended.
Untreated complete injuries progress predictably to scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC) arthritis over years.
Management differs sharply between an acute repairable ligament, a chronic reducible deformity without arthritis, and a chronic irreducible or arthritic wrist.
Arthroscopy remains the reference standard for staging partial versus complete tears when imaging is equivocal.
reference.pathophysiology: The scapholunate interosseous ligament, together with secondary stabilisers such as the dorsal intercarpal ligament, scaphotrapeziotrapezoid ligament and radioscaphocapitate ligament, maintains the tight kinematic linkage between scaphoid and lunate. When the dorsal scapholunate ligament and its secondary restraints fail, typically after a fall on the extended, ulnar-deviated and supinated wrist, the scaphoid loses restraint and rotates into flexion and pronation while the lunate, still tethered to the triquetrum, extends into a DISI posture. The resulting rotatory subluxation of the scaphoid concentrates load on the radioscaphoid articulation and initiates a predictable degenerative cascade.
additionalDifferentials: Distal radius fracture with associated ligament injury
Dorsal wrist ganglion or occult ganglion
additionalInvestigations: Standard PA, lateral and clenched-fist stress radiographs with contralateral comparison views
Measurement of the scapholunate gap and scapholunate angle on plain films
MRI focused on the scapholunate interosseous ligament
MR arthrography or CT arthrography to assess ligament integrity
Wrist arthroscopy for definitive staging using the Geissler classification
Fluoroscopic or cineradiographic dynamic motion studies
Grip-loaded views to provoke dynamic gapping
redFlags: Progressive dorsal wrist pain and loss of grip after a fall, suggesting evolving instability
Radiographic DISI or scapholunate gapping indicating complete ligament disruption
Early radioscaphoid narrowing or osteophytes signalling onset of SLAC collapse
High-energy mechanism with associated perilunate instability or dislocation
reference.prognosis: Acute, well-reduced injuries repaired before arthritis develops have the best functional outcome, whereas untreated complete tears progress over years to SLAC arthritis with pain and stiffness.
pitfalls: Dismissing the injury as a simple sprain and missing the window for primary ligament repair.
Relying only on static radiographs and overlooking dynamic instability.
Failing to notice scapholunate widening on a distal radius fracture film.
Attributing dorsal wrist pain solely to a ganglion.
Not comparing with the contralateral wrist, since scapholunate distances vary between individuals.
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
management: Repair the scapholunate interosseous ligament primarily, often with dorsal capsulodesis and temporary K-wire fixation, in acute reducible injuries
Reconstruct chronic reducible instability with tendon graft or capsulodesis techniques when direct repair is no longer feasible
Reserve salvage procedures such as proximal row carpectomy, scaphoid excision with four-corner fusion, or wrist fusion for established SLAC arthritis
Consider wrist denervation for pain relief when motion-preserving reconstruction is not possible
Follow surgery with a period of immobilisation and structured hand therapy to restore controlled motion
Refer promptly to a hand surgeon, as outcome is best when complete injuries are addressed before arthritis develops
